title: Detecting & Counting Missing Values with isna() and sum()
code:
import pandas as pd

# Student survey records with missing marks
students = pd.DataFrame({
    "Name": ["Arun", "Priya", "Rahul", "Meena"],
    "Age": [20, 19, 21, 20],
    "Mark": [85.0, None, 78.0, None]
})

print("Original DataFrame:")
print(students)

print("\nBoolean mask of missing values (isna):")
print(students.isna())

print("\nMissing values count per column:")
print(students.isna().sum())

print("\nAny missing values in 'Mark'?", students["Mark"].isna().any())
explanation: isna() identifies None/NaN cells and produces a boolean table (True for missing). Chaining .sum() counts missing values per column because True evaluates to 1 and False evaluates to 0.

title: Handling Missing Data: fillna() vs dropna()
code:
import pandas as pd

products = pd.DataFrame({
    "Item": ["Laptop", "Mouse", "Monitor", "Cable"],
    "Price": [55000.0, 650.0, None, 250.0],
    "Discount": [10.0, None, 5.0, None]
})

print("Original Product Table:")
print(products)

# Strategy A: Impute missing discounts with 0 and missing prices with the mean
filled_df = products.copy()
filled_df["Discount"] = filled_df["Discount"].fillna(0)
filled_df["Price"] = filled_df["Price"].fillna(filled_df["Price"].mean())
print("\nStrategy A: After fillna() (Imputation):")
print(filled_df)

# Strategy B: Remove incomplete rows entirely
dropped_df = products.dropna()
print("\nStrategy B: After dropna() (Row Deletion):")
print(dropped_df)
explanation: fillna() preserves sample size and substitutes missing entries with domain-appropriate values (0 or average). dropna() discards incomplete rows entirely.

title: Combining DataFrames with pd.concat() (Stacking)
code:
import pandas as pd

# Q1 and Q2 sales records
q1_sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "Region": ["North", "South"],
    "Revenue": [120000, 95000]
})

q2_sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "Region": ["East", "West"],
    "Revenue": [88000, 115000]
})

# Vertical concatenation (stacking rows)
combined_sales = pd.concat([q1_sales, q2_sales], ignore_index=True)
print("Combined Annual Sales (pd.concat):")
print(combined_sales)
explanation: pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True) stacks rows together vertically, creating a continuous sequential index 0..N-1 across both tables.

title: Relational Combining with pd.merge() on a Common Key
code:
import pandas as pd

# Students roster
students = pd.DataFrame({
    "StudentID": [101, 102, 103],
    "Name": ["Arun", "Priya", "Rahul"]
})

# Examination scores
marks = pd.DataFrame({
    "StudentID": [101, 102, 103],
    "Score": [88, 94, 76]
})

# Merge using the shared 'StudentID' key
report_card = pd.merge(students, marks, on="StudentID")
print("Merged Academic Report Card:")
print(report_card)
explanation: pd.merge(students, marks, on='StudentID') matches records where StudentID aligns across both DataFrames, producing a consolidated report card table.
